cards.title: Introduction to ASP.NET Core Structure
cards.content:
A well-organized ASP.NET Core solution follows the principles of Clean Architecture and Separation of Concerns. Typically, a robust enterprise application is broken down into multiple projects:

  • Core / Domain: Contains entities, interfaces, and business logic.
  • Infrastructure: Handles data access, EF Core, and external services.
  • Web / API: The presentation layer containing controllers, middleware, and Program.cs.

cards.title: The Role of Program.cs
cards.content:
In ASP.NET Core 6 and later, Program.cs serves as the single entry point for configuring both the Dependency Injection container and the HTTP request pipeline (Middleware).

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// Add services to the container.
builder.Services.AddControllers();

var app = builder.Build();

// Configure the HTTP request pipeline.
app.MapControllers();
app.Run();

options.text: Startup.cs is mandatory in ASP.NET Core 8.
Program.cs is the single entry point for configuration and middleware.
Global.asax is used to configure routing.
Web.config is required for IIS integration.

cards.title: The Middleware Pipeline
cards.content:
Middleware are components assembled into an application pipeline to handle requests and responses. Each component can choose whether to pass the request to the next component in the pipeline and can perform work before and after the next component.

Order matters significantly! For example, authentication middleware must be registered before authorization middleware.

content.text: In ASP.NET Core, authentication must always be placed {{blank_1}} authorization in the request pipeline.

cards.title: Dependency Injection Lifetimes
cards.content:
ASP.NET Core has built-in support for Dependency Injection (DI). Services can be registered with three different lifetimes:

  • Transient: Created each time they are requested. Best for lightweight, stateless services.
  • Scoped: Created once per client request (connection). Best for Entity Framework contexts.
  • Singleton: Created the first time they are requested and then every subsequent request uses the same instance.

pairs.right: Created once and shared across the lifetime of the application

cards.title: Solution Folders and Files
cards.content:
Standard files and folders in an API project include:

  • Controllers/ - Handles incoming HTTP requests.
  • Models/ - View models or data transfer objects (DTOs).
  • appsettings.json - Configuration settings like connection strings.
  • Properties/launchSettings.json - Local development profiles.

steps: Register services in the DI container via builder.Services
Configure the middleware pipeline using app.Use... methods

cards.title: Summary of ASP.NET Core Structure
cards.content:
You have completed the module on ASP.NET Core Structure. Key takeaways:

  • Keep your solution modular using separate class libraries for Domain, Infrastructure, and API.
  • Use Program.cs effectively for configuring DI and middleware.
  • Understand DI lifetimes (Transient, Scoped, Singleton) to prevent memory leaks and concurrency bugs.
  • Always mind the order of middleware execution.
